title: Probabilistic Game Theory of Euchre
body:
This project applies game theory to a single, concrete decision in Euchre. Playing the "Stick the Dealer" variant — where the dealer is forced to call a suit if everyone else passes — the dealer is stuck with a weak hand of all 9s and a 10 while a Jack sits flipped face-up. Should they pick up that Jack, or pass and hope someone else calls first? I built a probabilistic model to find the mathematically optimal answer.

With over 600 million ways to deal the cards, enumerating every case was impractical, so I modeled the game with probability distributions instead. I represented each player's hand strength with a Beta distribution and the tricks they would win with a conditional Beta-Binomial, then built payoff tables for every outcome. Working backward through the game's decision tree, I solved for the rollback equilibrium — the move each player makes assuming everyone else plays optimally.

The model's verdict: the dealer should pass. Picking up carries an expected payoff of −0.766 against −0.672 for passing — both negative, since a hand that weak is simply a losing position, but passing is the lesser of two evils. The analysis also highlighted how heavily each player's choice depends on information they don't have, since the opponents can never know how weak the dealer's hand truly is.

The project was an exercise in translating a messy, high-variance real-world problem into a tractable statistical model, and in using conditional distributions and expected-value reasoning to reach a defensible conclusion.
